first_draft.title: Alice, Bob, and the Missing Moon Bread
first_draft.text:
Bob was a ginger cat with four white socks and a sneeze that came out like a tiny trumpet. It arrived whenever he got excited. So when Alice padded into the kitchen one grey Saturday morning and found him nose-deep in the bread bin, she knew something was up.

"Bob," she whispered, "where is the moon bread?"

Grandma Rose had baked a crescent loaf that morning, golden and crackly, with a dusting of sugar on top. It had been cooling on the windowsill. Now the windowsill was empty, except for a few flakes of crust and one very guilty whisker.

Bob's ears flattened. "Pffft-CHOO!" he said. It was not an answer, but it was a very loud one.

Alice looked under the table. She looked behind the flour jar and inside the teapot. She even peeked into the washing basket, where a sock was snoring softly. No moon bread. Only a trail of golden crumbs leading out through the open back door, like a path of tiny stars.

"Follow the crumbs," Alice said. Bob's tail curled up like a question mark, and off they went.

The crumbs led down the garden path, past the wobbly bean poles and a dented watering can. At the bottom step sat a plump grey pigeon, pecking happily at the very middle of the moon.

Bob crouched low. His whiskers quivered. His nose wrinkled. Alice could feel a sneeze building up inside him, like a kettle about to whistle.

"Don't," Alice breathed. "Stay very still."

Bob pressed his lips together so hard that his face went squashed and funny. The sneeze grumbled and fizzed somewhere deep inside him.

Alice thought hard. A pigeon was not scared of a cat. A pigeon was only scared of sudden noises and quick feet. She pulled a heel of plain bread from her pocket, the crust she had been saving for the ducks. She crumbled it onto the path, one piece at a time, far from the step.

"Coo, coo," she murmured, sounding as much like a pigeon as she could.

The pigeon cocked its head. It hopped off the step. It hopped toward the crumbs. Plip, plop, plip. Bob's eyes went very wide. He crept forward one paw at a time, and when the pigeon was busy gobbling, Alice gently lifted the moon bread into her apron.

Then the sneeze escaped. "PFFFT-CHOOOO!"

The pigeon flapped away with a squawk, leaving behind one fat grey feather and a very surprised cat.

Alice laughed until she had to sit on the step. Bob sat beside her, looking proud and sorry all at once.

"Well," said Grandma Rose from the back doorway, drying her hands on her apron. She had heard every squawk. "A moon bread with a nibble taken out of it is still a moon bread, I suppose. And I have enough flour for another."

So they baked a second moon together. Alice shaped the dough into a crescent while Bob sat on a stool and kept his nose well away from the flour bag. He did not manage it. A puff of white drifted up like a little snowstorm, and Grandma said it was the finest snow she had seen all year.

That evening, when the sky had turned the color of plums, Alice curled up in bed. Bob settled at her feet with a rumbly purr. On the windowsill, the new moon bread sat cooling, a pale golden crescent against the dark glass.

Outside, the garden was still. The pigeon was asleep in the apple tree. The watering can had stopped dripping. The house grew quiet, and the quiet grew soft.

"Goodnight, Bob," Alice whispered.

Bob's purr went on and on, slow as a sleepy clock.

"Goodnight, moon."

request: Leo and his dog Rocket go on a treasure hunt in the backyard

first_draft.title: Leo and Rocket's Backyard Gold
first_draft.text:
Leo had a map, and the map had a secret. It was folded soft as an old sock, with a drawing of a palm tree, a wiggly river, and a big red X by the garden fence. 'Ahoy, Rocket!' Leo whispered. His dog thumped his tail so hard the kitchen floor shook.

Out in the yard, the grass was cool and silver with dew. Leo knelt by the picnic table and frowned at the last clue. A corner had torn away, and the important words were gone. Only a few letters were left: Find the sundial. Then follow the... and then nothing at all.

Leo marched across the lawn to the old sundial. Its metal arm cast a long, thin shadow over the grass. 'Which way, Captain?' Leo asked. Rocket sniffed the shadow, then sneezed so hard his ears flapped. Then he zoomed to the tomato patch and started digging like a steam shovel. Dirt flew over Leo's sneakers. 'Rocket, that's a worm, not a treasure!' Rocket wagged and dropped a soggy tennis ball at Leo's feet. 'Thanks, but we need the rest of the clue.'

They searched behind the shed, under the bird bath, and inside the wheelbarrow. Leo peeked into the empty flowerpots. Rocket checked the fence, bumped the watering can, and splashed them both with cold water. 'Splish!' Leo giggled, wiping his face. Still no clue. Leo sat on the bottom step and sighed. The sky had turned pink and orange, and the crickets began to sing.

Then Rocket trotted into his doghouse and came back with something in his mouth. It was a crumpled scrap of paper, chewed at one corner and smelling of dog biscuits. Leo smoothed it flat on his knee. In faded pencil, it said: When the sundial's shadow stretches long, dig beneath it. 'Rocket, you found the missing piece!' Leo cheered. Rocket barked so loudly that the cat next door poked its head over the fence to see what all the fuss was about.

They raced across the grass together, Leo's flashlight bouncing and Rocket's ears flopping. The sundial's shadow now stretched all the way to the big oak tree. Leo knelt down and scraped at the soft dirt with a plastic shovel. Rocket dug too, paws flying, sending a spray of earth into the air. Clunk! Something hard knocked against the shovel. They brushed away the dirt and found a small wooden chest, painted gold and tied with a red ribbon. Leo's heart thumped like a drum. He pulled off the ribbon and lifted the lid. Inside sat a chocolate coin wrapped in shiny foil, a black eye patch, and a bone-shaped biscuit for Rocket. Tucked underneath was a note in Mom's loopy handwriting: Captain Leo, the treasure is yours. Love, Mom and Dad. Leo laughed so hard his belly wiggled, and Rocket licked his nose.

Back inside, Leo wore his eye patch while Mom poured warm cocoa into mugs with marshmallows floating on top. Dad read the note again in his best pirate voice, and Rocket thumped his tail on the rug. Leo tucked his map and the gold chest beside his pillow. Then he climbed into bed, pulled the quilt up to his chin, and wiggled his toes under the warm blanket.

Outside, the stars blinked on, one by one. The crickets hummed softer now, and the oak tree whispered in the breeze. Rocket curled up at the foot of the bed with a long, happy sigh. Leo's eyelids grew heavy, and his yawn stretched wide.

'Goodnight, Rocket,' he whispered.

Rocket's tail thumped once, slowly.

Goodnight, little captain.

first_draft.text:
When the kitchen clock struck midnight, the refrigerator gave a long, rumbly yawn. Click! The little light blinked on. Inside, the vegetables began to whisper. "Tonight is the night," said Carrot Clementine, who was small, orange, and very good at wiggling. "The Midnight Crisper Party starts now!"

Clementine had planned it all week. She invited the peas, who giggled in pairs. She invited the broccoli, who wore a tiny green hat. She invited Leon the leek, who never took off his long woolly scarf. The cucumbers promised cucumber sandwiches. The mushrooms promised nothing, because mushrooms never promise anything.

Then the music began. Wheeeee-crackle-hoot! It came from Dolly the Radio, a silver speaker tucked beside the lettuce. Her songs wobbled like jelly on a skateboard. "Oh, pickles!" squeaked Clementine. "We cannot dance to jelly music!" Worse still, the dance floor was a flattened paper bag, and it had grown as lumpy as a potato, because a jar of pickles had leaned on it all afternoon.

Leon went first. He hopped onto Dolly and gave her a gentle bonk. Bonk! Dolly hiccupped into a polka, then flopped into a sleepy waltz. The peas tried rolling across the bag, but they bounced in every direction, boing, boing, boing, until they landed in a bowl of spinach. The radishes tried to stamp the lumps flat, but they were too round, and they rolled away with squeaks. Broccoli tried to lift the bag, but his hat slid over his eyes, and he bumped into the butter dish. Bump! Plip! The butter wobbled and wiggled.

Clementine tiptoed closer and listened hard. Dolly's wobble was not in her songs at all. It came from her feet. One foot was a bottle cap, and it was crooked, so it tipped her whole body to one side with every beat. "Dolly needs a steady floor," said Clementine, "and so does our dance!" Leon unwound his long green scarf and tucked it under Dolly's crooked cap, like a soft cushion. Dolly sat level at last. Then the cucumbers gently patted the paper bag with their cool, flat sides, smoothing bump after bump. The mushrooms, who had promised nothing, rolled up the edges so no lumps could hide. The pickles scooched over with a polite, "Excuse me, excuse me."

Dolly played a clear, bouncy song. Everyone danced. The peas spun in circles, the radishes hopped, and Leon waltzed with his scarf back around his neck. Clementine did her best carrot wiggle. Nobody tripped, because there were no lumps left to trip on.

Now the party grew soft and slow. The music turned into a gentle hum. The dancers rolled to a stop, one by one. Leon tucked his scarf around his shoulders. The peas curled up together in a little green pod. Clementine gave a small orange yawn. "Good night, fridge," she whispered. The little light blinked off. Click. Somewhere in the dark, the refrigerator hummed a lullaby, and the vegetables drifted off to sleep until morning.

first_draft.title: Pim and the Vanishing Honey Cake
first_draft.text:

When Pim came back, the windowsill was empty. Only three crumbs were left, and a trail of sticky dots led across the floor, under the table, and out through a crack in the door.

"Mystery!" whispered Pim, pulling on his scarf. Snail climbed slowly onto Pim's back, and they followed the trail through the long grass. It wobbled past the mushroom house, then past the pond, where a frog blinked at them in surprise. "Have you seen a cake?" asked Pim. The frog only croaked and hopped away.

Pim felt cross and worried at the same time. Grandmother Fern would be arriving at sunset, and the cake was meant to be her special treat. "Maybe we should give up," Pim sighed. Snail stopped, leaned close to the grass, and said, "Wait. Look at these dots. They're smaller than crumbs. And there's something sparkly in the middle."

They crept along. The trail led to a hollow log, and from inside came a small, squeaky giggle. Pim tiptoed up and peeked in. Three baby dormice sat in a nest of moss, their cheeks round and sticky with honey. Between them lay a lopsided piece of cake, with one very big bite out of it.

"You took our cake!" Pim said, then his voice softened. "Did you want some?" The smallest dormouse hiccupped. "It smelled so good," she whispered. "Mama's out looking for berries, and we were hungry." Pim's ears drooped, then perked up again.

Pim thought for a moment. "Snail, what if we bring the rest to Grandmother Fern's party? We could bring the dormice too, and some berries from the bush." Snail nodded slowly, and his shell gave a happy little wobble. "I'll carry the plates," he said. "Carefully."

So they gathered blackberries, and the baby dormice trotted along behind them, holding tight to Pim's scarf. When Grandmother Fern arrived, the garden was full of twinkling lanterns, and the table was covered in cake, berries, and a surprise or two. Grandmother Fern laughed until her spectacles fogged up. "My favourite guests," she said.

Late that night, when the lanterns had dimmed and the owl had begun to hoot softly, Pim tucked the last blanket around the dormice's nest. Snail curled up beside the pillow, his shell glowing faintly in the moonlight.

The wind stopped. The crickets stopped. Everything grew quiet, the way a garden does when it is nearly asleep.

Pim gave a small, crinkly yawn. Outside, the pond lay still and silver, and the moon rolled slowly over the hill.

Goodnight, Pim. Goodnight, Snail. Goodnight, sleepy dormice, tucked in tight.

first_draft.text:
In the tall oak wood, there lived a hedgehog named Prickles. Prickles loved to bake. Today was Grandmother Owl's birthday, and Prickles had a very special cake to make.

Stir, stir, round and round! Splish, splash, splosh! Prickles' spoon sang around the big blue bowl.

Mole came hopping up the path. Duck came waddling behind him. "We are here to help!" they said.

Mole reached for the jar on the top shelf. "Sugar!" he said, and he shook a big scoop into the bowl.

Prickles tasted the batter. Her nose wrinkled. Her whiskers drooped. "Yuck! This tastes like the sea!"

"Salt!" squeaked Mole. "I took the wrong jar!"

Duck flapped his wings. "Then we need more sweet!" He poured in a whole pot of honey. SPLOOSH! The batter got sticky, and Duck's feet stuck to the floor. "Quack! I'm glued!"

Rabbit hopped in with plums. One bounced off the table and landed right on Mole's nose. BONK!

Stir, stir, round and round! Everybody sang, while Duck wiggled and wobbled and wiggled some more.

Prickles sat down. Her quills drooped low. Then she sniffed the two jars. One smelled like the sea. The other smelled like sunshine.

"Mole," she said, "the sea jar is salt. The sunshine jar is sugar. It was on the top shelf the whole time."

Mole covered his face with his paws. "Oops," he mumbled, and everyone giggled. Duck gave a big wiggle and went POP! He was free.

Prickles shaped the salty batter into crunchy biscuits for the birds. Then she mixed a fresh bowl, with the right jar.

Stir, stir, round and round! Into the oven it went, and out came a golden cake that smelled of plums and honey.

Grandmother Owl hooted with delight. "Best birthday ever," she said, and she ate two slices.

The friends sat in the soft grass, yawning. The sun sank low behind the trees.

The wood grew quiet and still. A soft breeze hummed through the leaves. Prickles tucked her quills in close. Goodnight, little wood. Goodnight, sweet cake.

first_draft.title: Gobbleshy and the Lost Red Mitten
first_draft.text:
Under the old apple tree, behind the blue gate, lived a monster named Gobbleshy. He had soft gray fur, two round eyes like warm buttons, and a very big appetite for cookies and socks. Gobbleshy was also very shy, so he only ate in the dark, where nobody could hear him crunch.

One frosty morning, Nell pulled on her wellies and reached for her red mitten. It was gone. "Mittens do not walk away by themselves," said Grandad, rubbing his whiskery chin. "Somebody must have borrowed it." Nell wiggled her bare fingers. The wind was sharp, and her hand felt like an icicle.

Nell searched the porch, the shed, and under the wooden bench. Then she spotted a trail of crumbs leading across the frosty grass toward the blue gate. The crumbs smelled of ginger and warm butter. "Follow the crumbs," Nell whispered, and she tiptoed along, step by careful step.

At the old apple tree, a loud hiccup came from under the roots. Nell knelt in the wet leaves. "Hello?" she called softly. "Is someone there?" There was a rustle, then a wobbly voice. "Please don't look at me. I'm too shy to be looked at."

Nell sat down on the cold grass and crossed her legs. "I'll wait," she said. "Take as long as you need." After a long moment, two round eyes peeked out from the roots. Gobbleshy held a striped sock in one paw and a half-eaten cookie in the other. His ears drooped low.

"I didn't eat your mitten," he said in a small voice. "I found it under the hedge last night. It looked so cold and lonely, all by itself. first_draft.text:
The house on Pennywhistle Lane had a ghost, and everyone knew it, because the ghost hiccupped. Hic! went the banisters. Hic! went the teapot lids. Hic! went the windows, rattling like teeth in a cold mouth.

On the night Ethan and his cousin Nell came to stay at Gran's, the hiccups were loudest of all. Nell pulled her quilt up to her nose. "It's the ghost," she whispered. "He's been hiccupping since Tuesday." Ethan wanted to say that ghosts were made up, but a candle flame bowed low, as if someone had breathed on it, and a sound rolled down the stairs: hic, hic, HIC!

"Gran will know what to do," said Ethan, and he was already tiptoeing into the hall, his slippers slapping softly on the boards. Gran was in the kitchen, stirring cocoa with a wooden spoon. She didn't even look up. "Hollis again? Up in the attic, poor thing. Take the lantern, and mind the third step. It creaks like a grumpy old goose."

Up the narrow stairs they went, lantern swinging, dust floating like slow snow. In the attic, under the rafters, sat a ghost wrapped in a patchwork quilt. He was pale and wobbly, with eyes like two drips of candle wax. "Hic," said Hollis miserably. "Sorry. Hic. I was going to say Boo."

"Boo-hic!" Nell giggled, then clapped a hand over her mouth. Hollis puffed out his cheeks and tried to hold his breath. He swelled up like a balloon, floated right off the floor, and bumped gently against the ceiling beam. Then he let out a squeaky "Hic!" and sank back down, looking embarrassed.

"Water," said Ethan sensibly. Nell fetched a glass from the kitchen, and they tipped it over Hollis's head. The water passed straight through him and splashed Ethan's slippers. "Oops," said Ethan. Hollis hiccupped so hard that the lantern wobbled, and a shadow ran across the wall like a startled mouse.

Ethan sat down on an old trunk and thought hard. Gran always said hiccups came when you were too excited. "What were you doing before they started?" he asked. Hollis sniffed. "Laughing at a sock. It floated past my nose and looked so silly, I couldn't help it. Hic!"

"A sock," said Nell. "Right. Then we need something extremely boring." Ethan cleared his throat. "Wallpaper," he began in a slow, flat voice. "Beige stripes. Then more beige stripes. Then the stripes between the stripes, which go up, and then down, and then, well, more stripes."

Hollis's eyes drooped. His mouth opened wide, and out came an enormous yawn. "Hoooaaahhh." He waited. Not one single hiccup. "Oh," he whispered. "Oh, it worked."

Nell and Ethan cheered in whispers, so they wouldn't wake the rafters. Hollis tugged a little silver bell from under his quilt and gave it a gentle shake. It made a sound like someone humming in another room. "This is for you," he said. "It rings only when the house is safe for dreaming."

Gran's voice floated up the stairs. "Cocoa's ready, you two!" Hollis waved his misty hand, and the lantern flame stood up tall and straight. Downstairs, the cocoa was warm and sweet, and the windows had stopped their rattling.

Later, in the blue quiet of the guest room, Ethan lay with the silver bell on his pillow. The house creaked once, softly. Then it didn't creak at all. Far above, a sleepy little hiccup drifted down like a feather. Ethan smiled into his blanket. The stairs were still. The moon was small and silver. The whole house sighed, and settled, and slept.

Goodnight, Pennywhistle Lane. Goodnight, Hollis. Goodnight.

first_draft.text:
On the edge of Puddlewick Meadow, where the stream giggled over smooth pebbles, lived a very small knight named Sir Pim. His armor clinked when he walked, his helmet was one size too big, and his sword, called Whistle, hummed a tiny tune whenever it swished through the air.

One morning, Sir Pim woke to a sound he did not like. Crunch. Creak. Snap-snap-snap.

He pulled on his boots, tugged his helmet over his ears, and hurried outside. His best friend, Moss, a green dragon as round as a haystack, was already standing in the lane, blinking at the gloomy heap in front of him.

Overnight, a tangle of thorny brambles had grown right across the path. Its vines were knotted as tightly as a ball of yarn after a kitten has played with it for an hour.

On the other side of the brambles sat Mrs. Crumb's cart, piled high with honey buns for the Puddlewick picnic. The wheels were stuck. The buns were getting cold. And the picnic would begin very soon.

"Leave it to me!" said Moss. He grabbed a thorny vine in his big claws. "Heave-ho!"

The vine pulled back. Moss pulled harder. The brambles pulled harder still, and Moss tumbled backward into the stream. SPLOOSH!

Sir Pim giggled so hard that his helmet wobbled. "My turn," he said. He lifted his shield and pushed against the thorns. BONK! The shield bounced off, and Sir Pim sat down with a surprised "oof."

Mrs. Crumb leaned out of her cottage window, a warm bun in one hand. "Oh, my dears," she called. "Those knots are very tight indeed."

Sir Pim looked closely at the tangle. Some knots were lumpy and loose. Others were small and hard as peas. Every time someone pushed or pulled, the knots squeezed tighter.

"Maybe thorns don't like to be shoved," he said slowly. "Maybe they like to be knocked, like a friend at the door."

He drew Whistle from its sheath. Tik. Tok. Tik. He tapped the first knot, very gently, and it gave a soft little ring, like a tiny bell. The knot wiggled. Tok. Tok. Tik. The second knot sighed and loosened, and a small loop slipped free.

Moss climbed out of the stream, dripping and puffing, and held the cart's wheel with one claw so it could not roll backward. "Good thinking, Pim," he said. "Keep going, but slowly."

Sir Pim tapped the next knot, and the next, and the next. Each one loosened with a sleepy sigh, until the brambles lay in long, untangled ribbons across the lane.

"Now!" squeaked Sir Pim.

Moss pushed. Sir Pim pushed. The cart rolled free with a happy rattle-rattle-rattle, and the honey buns bounced in their basket.

Mrs. Crumb clapped her floury hands. "Just in time for the picnic!"

That afternoon, everyone sat on the soft grass and ate sticky buns. Moss sneezed a puff of warm smoke that made the ducks squawk, and the whole meadow laughed until the sun grew tired and gold.

When evening came, the stream began its old song, hushing over the pebbles. Moss curled up beside the meadow like a warm green hill and let out a long, rumbly snore. Sir Pim hung his helmet on a branch and laid Whistle gently in the grass.

The stars came out, one by one.

Tik... tok... went the stream.

Tik... tok... went the stream, softer now.

Goodnight, Sir Pim. Goodnight, Moss. Goodnight, little stream, humming, humming, hushing, hush.

first_draft.title: Maya and the Puddle Frog
first_draft.text:
Maya's shoes squeaked on the shiny hall floor of Pine Hill School. Her tummy felt like a jar of fizzy lemonade. It was Monday, and it was her very first day.

She gripped her backpack straps. She looked at the bright posters and the rows of pegs. Everyone else seemed to know exactly where they were going.

Mrs. Osei hung Maya's coat on a hook shaped like a duck. 'Class, this is Maya,' she said. 'Say hello, Maya.' Maya waved. Thirty eyes looked at her. Her cheeks went warm as toast.

'Hello,' Maya tried to say. It came out as a tiny squeak, like a mouse with a cold. Nobody heard. Maya sat by the window and kept her hands very still.

At break, the big girls were turning a long rope. Slap, slap, slap went the rope on the playground. 'Cherry on top, cherry on top!' they chanted, jumping and jumping.

Maya stood at the edge with her toes on the line. She wanted to jump. She wanted to chant. But her feet stayed stuck to the tarmac like gum on a shoe. Nobody asked her to come in.

So she walked to the bench by the fence. She counted the clouds. One, two, three, four, five. A pigeon strutted past, pitter-patter, pitter-patter. Maya let out a sigh as big as a balloon.

After lunch came art. Maya reached for a blue crayon. Her fingers slipped. The crayon rolled off the table, bumpity-bump, and stopped under the desk next to her.

A boy with curly hair bent down and picked it up. His name tag said Theo in wobbly letters. He held out the crayon without a word, and his ears turned pink.

'Thanks,' whispered Maya. 'Is it yours?'

Theo shook his head. 'It's puddle blue,' he whispered back. 'I like puddles.'

'Me too,' said Maya. 'The jumpy kind.'

Theo drew a frog with big round eyes and a wide smile. Maya took a green crayon and gave the frog a tiny red bow tie. Theo giggled, a squeaky giggle, and she giggled back.

'Ribbit, ribbit, hello,' Theo whispered to his frog. Maya whispered it to hers too.

At break, Maya did not stand at the edge. She walked straight to the bench where Theo sat with his picture. 'Can I sit here?' she asked. Theo scooted over so fast his shoe bumped the bench.

'Do you want to hop?' he asked, nodding at the rope.

Maya looked at the rope. Then she looked at Theo. 'Maybe next time,' she said. 'Today I want to draw more frogs.' Theo grinned so wide she could see his gap tooth.

When the bell rang, Mrs. Osei smiled at their paper. 'What a lively pond,' she said. Maya tucked the frog picture into her bag. Her tummy did not feel like lemonade anymore. It felt like a warm bath.

Dad was waiting at the gate with his big yellow umbrella. 'How was it?' he asked.

Maya thought about the bow tie and the puddle crayon. 'Good,' she said. 'I think I found a frog.'

That night the moon hung like a soft white coin in the window. The frog picture sat on her shelf, its bow tie bright. The house was quiet. Her blanket was warm and heavy.

Hop, hop, goodnight, she whispered.

Ribbit, said the frog on the paper.

Hush, said the wind.

The moon sank slowly down. Maya's eyes closed. One, two, three.

Ribbit. Goodnight.

final.title: Maya and the Puddle Frog
final.text:
Maya's shoes squeaked on the shiny hall floor of Pine Hill School. Her tummy felt like a jar of fizzy lemonade. It was Monday, and it was her very first day.

She gripped her backpack straps. She looked at the bright posters and the rows of pegs. Everyone else seemed to know exactly where they were going.

Mrs. Osei hung Maya's coat on a hook shaped like a duck. 'Class, this is Maya,' she said. 'Say hello, Maya.' Maya waved. Thirty eyes looked at her. Her cheeks went warm as toast.

'Hello,' Maya tried to say. It came out as a tiny squeak, like a mouse with a cold. Nobody heard. Maya sat by the window and kept her hands very still.

At break, the big girls were turning a long rope. Slap, slap, slap went the rope on the playground. 'Cherry on top, cherry on top!' they chanted, jumping and jumping.

Maya stood at the edge with her toes on the line. She wanted to jump. She wanted to chant. But her feet stayed stuck to the tarmac like gum on a shoe. Nobody asked her to come in.

So she walked to the bench by the fence. She counted the clouds. One, two, three, four, five. A pigeon strutted past, pitter-patter, pitter-patter. Maya let out a sigh as big as a balloon.

After lunch came art. Maya reached for a blue crayon. Her fingers slipped. The crayon rolled off the table, bumpity-bump, and stopped under the desk next to her.

A boy with curly hair bent down and picked it up. His name tag said Theo in wobbly letters. He held out the crayon without a word, and his ears turned pink.

'Thanks,' whispered Maya. 'Is it yours?'

Theo shook his head. 'It's puddle blue,' he whispered back. 'I like puddles.'

'Me too,' said Maya. 'The jumpy kind.'

Theo drew a frog with big round eyes and a wide smile. Maya took a green crayon and gave the frog a tiny red bow tie. Theo giggled, a squeaky giggle, and she giggled back.

'Ribbit, ribbit, hello,' Theo whispered to his frog. Maya whispered it to hers too.

At break, Maya did not stand at the edge. She walked straight to the bench where Theo sat with his picture. 'Can I sit here?' she asked. Theo scooted over so fast his shoe bumped the bench.

'Do you want to hop?' he asked, nodding at the rope.

Maya looked at the rope. Then she looked at Theo. 'Maybe next time,' she said. 'Today I want to draw more frogs.' Theo grinned so wide she could see his gap tooth.

When the bell rang, Mrs. Osei smiled at their paper. 'What a lively pond,' she said. Maya tucked the frog picture into her bag. Her tummy did not feel like lemonade anymore. It felt like a warm bath.

Dad was waiting at the gate with his big yellow umbrella. 'How was it?' he asked.

Maya thought about the bow tie and the puddle crayon. 'Good,' she said. 'I think I found a frog.'

That night the moon hung like a soft white coin in the window. The frog picture sat on her shelf, its bow tie bright. The house was quiet. Her blanket was warm and heavy.

Hop, hop, goodnight, she whispered.

Ribbit, said the frog on the paper.

Hush, said the wind.

The moon sank slowly down. Maya's eyes closed. One, two, three.

Ribbit. Goodnight.

first_draft.title: The Squeaky Duck on the Windowsill
first_draft.text:
The house was very quiet that night. Sam lay under his blue blanket and listened. He listened for the jingle of Biscuit's tag. He listened for the thump, thump, thump of a tail against the hallway floor. He heard only the tick of the clock and the hum of the fridge downstairs. Biscuit had gone to sleep for good last week, and Sam still waited for him every night.

Creak. The door opened a crack. Grandpa padded in wearing his fuzzy slippers, the ones that went shhh, shhh across the carpet. He carried two mugs of cocoa, and the steam smelled of cinnamon.

"Can't sleep, Sam?"

"It's too quiet," Sam whispered. "I keep waiting for him to come bumping up the stairs."

Grandpa sat on the edge of the bed. The mattress sagged with a squeak. "I miss him too. He snored like a rusty gate."

"And he stole socks," said Sam. "He hid them under the couch."

"Forty-two socks, I counted once," said Grandpa, and Sam giggled into his cocoa.

Sam tried counting sheep. One sheep. Two sheep. Three sheep wearing tiny hats. Then he pictured Biscuit chasing a sheep-shaped cloud across the garden, and he lost count completely. He tried tucking his feet under the pillow. He tried humming. Each time, the quiet crept back in, like a cat looking for a warm spot.

Then Sam's toe bumped something hard under the bed. He wiggled down and felt around. His fingers closed on something soft and rubbery. He pulled it out. It was Biscuit's yellow duck. Sam gave it a squeeze. SQUEAK! Squeak-squeak! The sound was so bouncy and silly that Sam let out a surprised laugh. Then his eyes went wobbly.

Grandpa's eyes went soft too. "That duck went everywhere with him," he said. "Even to the bath, where he always tried to join in."

Sam tucked the duck under his chin. "I don't want it under the bed," he said. "And I don't want it in the toy box. It would be lonely there."

Grandpa rubbed his beard. "Where would Biscuit like it best?"

Sam looked around the room. His eyes landed on the window, where the moon was peeking in like a silver coin. "There," he said. "On the windowsill, so it can watch the moon with us."

They set the duck on the windowsill. Then Sam had an idea. He grabbed his box of crayons, and Grandpa held the paper flat while Sam drew. He drew floppy ears, a wagging tail, and one very large sock in Biscuit's mouth. The tail was a little wobbly, but Grandpa said it looked exactly right.

They taped the drawing to the wall beside the door, at the height where a dog's nose would be. Sam leaned close and whispered, "Goodnight, Biscuit." Then he gave the duck one soft squeeze. Squeak. The house still felt quiet, but it was a different kind of quiet now. A warm one.

Grandpa turned off the lamp. The room turned silver and blue. Sam pulled his blanket up and sipped the last of his cocoa, slow and warm. The clock ticked. The fridge hummed. Far away, an owl said hoo, hoo, softly.

The duck sat on the windowsill, glowing in the moonlight. The drawing watched over the door. The house settled, one creak at a time.

Sam's eyes grew heavy. His breathing slowed. Shh, said the night.

Goodnight, Sam.

first_draft.title: Hazel and the Humming Night
first_draft.text:
Once upon a time, in a tall oak tree at the edge of Whispering Wood, there lived a sleepy owl named Hazel.

Hazel yawned a big, round yawn. "Hoo-hoo-hoo," she sighed. Her eyes felt as heavy as wet leaves.

"Time to go home to my hollow," said Hazel. "Home is soft with moss and feathers."

But the moon had slipped behind a cloud, and the wood looked different. The path looked like a long, dark ribbon. Hazel blinked. Which way was home?

Down below, a little mouse named Pip peeked out from under a fern. "Are you lost, Hazel?"

"Only a little," Hazel said, and her voice came out soft. "All the trees look the same, and I am so very sleepy."

Pip wiggled his whiskers. "Let's listen. Quiet helps us find things."

So they sat very still. A brook gurgled over smooth stones. Splish, splash, splosh. A breeze sighed through the grass. Shhh, shhh.

Hazel closed her eyes and remembered the song her mother used to hum. She hummed it low and slow. Hmmm... hmmm...

From far away, a gentle answer came back. Hmmm... hmmm... It was the frogs by the pond, singing their evening song.

"The pond is near the big oak," Pip said, pointing with a tiny paw. "Follow the hum!"

Hazel flapped her soft wings, one, two, slow and quiet. Over the ferns she glided, past the brook, under the silver moon that peeked out again. Soon she saw her tall oak standing beside the pond.

"Thank you, Pip," she whispered.

Pip giggled. "Goodnight, Hazel."

Hazel settled into her hollow. The moss was warm. The feathers were soft. She tucked her head under one wing.

Hoo... hoo... the wood said, very softly.

Outside, the brook kept up its quiet splashing. The breeze rocked the leaves. The frogs hummed, and the moon hummed, and the little owl hummed too.

Hmmm... hmmm...

Hazel's eyes closed, one and then the other.

Now the wood is still. The stars blink slow. Everything is hushed, and everything is sleeping.

Goodnight, little owl. Goodnight, little one. Hmm... hoo...

first_draft.title: Zoe and the Humming Crystal
first_draft.text:
Zoe Hart had a tortoise named Pebble, and Pebble had a very stubborn habit of stopping for everything. One sunny Saturday they climbed the grassy hill behind Grandpa Joe's cottage, past the wild thyme and the buzzing bees, until they reached a crack in the rocks. Cool air breathed out of it, smelling of wet stone and rain.

"Stay where I can see you," said Grandpa Joe, leaning on his walking stick. "We'll peek in together." Zoe clicked on her flashlight. Pebble, who never liked to be rushed, decided the crack looked like a fine place for a snack. He poked his nose inside, and then the rest of him followed. Scritch, scrape, scritch, went his claws across the stones.

"Pebble, wait!" Zoe squeezed through after him. The passage opened into a round cave, and Zoe forgot to breathe. Pale green crystals grew from the walls like frozen fireworks. When her flashlight beam touched them, it split into a hundred tiny rainbows that danced across the ceiling.

Then she heard it. A low hum, soft as a cat purring, came from the middle of the floor. In a hollow lay a crystal as big as a loaf of bread, glowing a warm honey gold. Each time it hummed, the light pulsed, and the walls sparkled brighter. "Grandpa!" she whispered. "Come see! It's singing!"

Grandpa Joe ducked inside, his eyes wide as saucers. "Well, I'll be. I've walked this hill for sixty years and never found this." Zoe knelt beside the crystal. It was warm, like a mug of cocoa on a cold morning, and it hummed right up through her fingertips. She wanted it more than anything. She imagined it on her windowsill at home, humming her to sleep every night. Maybe nobody else would ever need to know. Quietly, while Grandpa was looking at the ceiling, she broke off a small golden chip, no bigger than a button, and slipped it into her pocket.

The hum stopped. Just like that, the golden light faded to a dim, sleepy glow. The rainbows slid off the ceiling and vanished. Zoe's tummy went cold and heavy. She pulled out the chip. It felt cold in her palm now, and it was not humming at all.

"Grandpa," she said in a small voice, "I think I did something wrong." Grandpa Joe sat down on a flat stone and patted the space beside him. Zoe told him everything, and her cheeks went hot as toast. Grandpa was quiet for a moment. "This cave has been keeping its song for a very long time," he said at last. "It's like a garden. We can look and enjoy the flowers, but we shouldn't carry them home in our pockets."

Zoe tried to think. Pebble bumped gently against her boot, as if he were thinking too. "Maybe it needs to go home," she said slowly. She knelt by the hollow and held the chip in both hands. It was so small. Carefully, she pressed it back into the gap where it had broken off. Nothing happened at first. Her heart thumped. She waited, counting slow breaths. One, two, three.

Then, with a soft tick, the chip settled into place. The hum came back, warm and low, and the golden glow swelled until the whole cave shimmered like the inside of a sunrise. The rainbows returned to dance across the ceiling. Pebble stretched out his wrinkly neck and blinked happily. "Thank you," Zoe whispered to the crystal, and it hummed a little louder, as if it had heard her.

Grandpa Joe smiled. "Finding something wonderful is a gift, Zoe. Sharing it is good too, but looking after it is the best part of all." Zoe nodded slowly. "Next time I'll tell my class about it, and we can all come up and look together. We'll only look, though. Some treasures are best left right where they are. Taking care of a place is part of loving it."

They climbed out into the afternoon, where the hill was golden and the bees were humming their own little songs. Pebble took his time on every blade of grass, and Zoe waited for him, not once tapping her feet.

That evening, the cottage was quiet. Pebble snored softly in his cozy box by the window. Zoe lay under her quilt and thought about the crystal, humming alone in the dark hill, keeping its gold light for whoever came to visit next. Her eyelids grew heavy. The wind sighed through the thyme, and the moon rose slow and silver.

"Goodnight, little song," Zoe whispered.

Far away, under the hill, the crystal hummed back, softly, softly, softly.
